input: Given /data/team_a.txt and /data/team_b.txt containing member names (one per line, already sorted), use the comm command to find: 1) Members only in Team A (print under 'Only Team A:'). 2) Members only in Team B (print under 'Only Team B:'). 3) Members in both teams (print under 'Both teams:'). Print the count of each group.

transcript.final_response:
I compared the two files with `comm`. Since both files were already sorted, they didn't need sorting first.

```bash
cd /data
a=$(comm -23 team_a.txt team_b.txt)   # only in A (hide columns 2 & 3)
b=$(comm -13 team_a.txt team_b.txt)   # only in B (hide columns 1 & 3)
c=$(comm -12 team_a.txt team_b.txt)   # in both  (hide columns 1 & 2)
cnt(){ [ -z "$1" ] && echo 0 || printf '%s\n' "$1" | wc -l | tr -d ' '; }

echo "Only Team A:"; printf '%s\n' "$a"; echo "Count: $(cnt "$a")"; echo
echo "Only Team B:"; printf '%s\n' "$b"; echo "Count: $(cnt "$b")"; echo
echo "Both teams:";  printf '%s\n' "$c"; echo "Count: $(cnt "$c")"
```

**Output:**
```
Only Team A:
alice
dave
eve
Count: 3

Only Team B:
frank
grace
Count: 2

Both teams:
bob
carol
Count: 2
```

`comm` puts its output in three columns: lines only in the first file, lines only in the second file, and lines in both. The `-1`, `-2` and `-3` flags hide those columns, so each command above keeps just one group. The `cnt` helper returns 0 when a group is empty, because a plain `wc -l` would count the empty line as 1.
